title: Custom type kinds (class, struct, record, and more)
hook: Beyond `int` and `string`, C# lets you declare your own types — classes, structs, records, interfaces, enums, and more. This page is a map of what exists, not a full object-oriented lesson.

blocks.text: When built-in types are not enough, you **declare your own types**. A **class** is a reference type with identity — two instances are different even with the same data. A **struct** is a value type that copies on assignment. A **record** (class or struct) adds compiler-generated equality and `with` expressions. An **interface** is a contract with no fields of its own. An **enum** names integer constants. A **tuple** groups values without inventing a type name: `(string id, int attempts)`. **Generics** like `List<T>` let you write types with placeholders.

entries.plainDefinition: A reference type you create with `new`. Instances have identity — same data, different objects, unless you override equality.
A value type you define. Assignment copies all fields. Cannot inherit from another struct or class (except interfaces).
A class or struct with compiler-generated equality, `ToString`, and `with` copy expressions. Good for data-centric types.
A named set of integer constants. Under the hood it is a value type based on `int` (by default).

blocks.text: Picking the wrong kind causes pain later. A mutable **struct** in a `List<T>` leads to copy surprises. An **enum** for open-ended auth provider names breaks when a new provider appears. A **tuple** leaking across five methods should become a named **record**. An SQS message envelope is a **class** or **record** (identity and lifecycle). A color with Red/Green/Blue is a small **struct**. A cache policy is an **enum**. A `(score, weight)` pair while parsing CSV is a **tuple** until it grows into a type.

blocks.title: Heuristic
blocks.body: Same data should mean the same thing? → **record** or small **struct**. Unique identity or lifecycle (dispose, mutate internal state)? → **class**. Behavior contract shared by unrelated types? → **interface**.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Need identity or shared mutable state?
items.body: Choose **class** (or **record class**). Example: `SqsEnvelope` with a `Body` property that handlers mutate or log.

items.title: Small, copy-friendly, no identity?
items.body: Choose **struct** or **record struct**. Example: `Grade` with a single `decimal Value`.

items.title: Temporary pair inside one method?
items.body: Choose **tuple**. Promote to a named type when it crosses method boundaries.

diagram.title: Custom type kind map
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  Q{"What are you modeling?"}
  Q -->|identity / lifecycle| CL["class or record class"]
  Q -->|small copyable data| ST["struct or record struct"]
  Q -->|fixed constants| EN["enum"]
  Q -->|shared behavior| IF["interface"]
  Q -->|quick local pair| TU["tuple"]
  Q -->|reusable container| GE["generic List<T>"]

snippet.label: Catalog in one glance
snippet.explanation: Line 1: enum for a closed set. Line 3: record struct for a copyable grade value. Lines 5–8: class for a message with identity. Lines 10–13: interface for a contract. Line 15: tuple for a quick pair — promote when it spreads.

snippet.label: Record with expression and with-copy
snippet.explanation: Line 3: records get value-based equality by default. Line 4: `with` creates a shallow copy with changed fields — `ada` is untouched. Line 6: equality compares all properties, not reference identity.

snippet.label: Generic list as a reusable container
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `List<T>` is a generic reference type — `T` is replaced with `Grade` at compile time. No boxing, full type safety. Inheritance, virtual methods, and members are covered in later modules.

blocks.title: Type constructors
rows: No struct — use object or library

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Mutable structs in collections — assignment copies bite. Enums for open-ended string issuers from auth providers — a class or constants may fit better. Treating interface as something you `new` — interfaces are contracts, not concrete types.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: `readonly struct` (C# 7.2+) prevents accidental mutation after construction — the compiler rejects writes to instance fields outside constructors. Pair it with `readonly record struct` for small immutable values like grades, coordinates, or cache keys. In hot paths, `readonly struct` passed with `in` avoids defensive copies that mutable structs trigger. Prefer `record class` for DTOs that cross service boundaries; `readonly record struct` for in-process numeric wrappers.

snippet.label: readonly struct versus mutable struct trap
snippet.explanation: Line 1: readonly record struct — immutable by design. Line 7: `in Grade` avoids copying a small readonly struct. Lines 9–11: mutable struct in a list — classic copy trap from value-vs-reference topic.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Tiny numeric wrappers that copy constantly
Open-ended string codes from external APIs
Crosses more than one method boundary

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying struct is always faster than class without mentioning copy cost. Using mutable structs in collections without explaining the indexer copy trap. Picking enum for auth issuer strings that grow weekly. Claiming records replace classes for everything.

interviewTakeaways: class vs struct is reference vs value — size alone is not the rule.
readonly struct and readonly record struct prevent mutation and enable in parameters.
records add value equality; tuples should become named types when they leak.
60s: readonly record struct for small immutable values. class for identity. enum for closed sets. Promote tuples to records.
Follow-up: why does List<MutableStruct>[i].X = 1 fail to update the list?
commonPitfalls: Mutable structs in collections without explaining copy semantics gets you rejected.
Saying struct is always faster — large struct copies hurt.
Strong answer: 'readonly record struct for immutable values. class for lifecycle. enum for closed constants. Know the list indexer copy trap.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript interfaces and type aliases erase at run time. C# interfaces remain in metadata. TypeScript `enum` can emit run-time objects; C# enums are value types.
